The computational domain modeled a straight duct with a square cross-section, roughened by square sharp-angled ribs.
The numerical simulations used Large Eddy Simulation (LES) to resolve the turbulent flow and heat transfer.
The grid had around 10 million computational cells with boundary layer resolution.
The Enhancement Factor (EF) was defined as the ratio of local heat transfer coefficient on the ribbed wall to the smooth wall.
The study identified key flow features such as separation zones, secondary recirculation regions, and coherent structures around the ribs.
Advanced post-processing techniques like Q-criterion, Principal Component Analysis, and Conditional Averaging were used to investigate the role of coherent structures.
The addition of cooling holes significantly altered the flow field and heat transfer, with changes in the downstream recirculation regions and secondary flows.
The numerical results were validated against experimental data, including measurements of pressure drop, flow field characteristics, and local heat transfer coefficients.
The study found that coherent structures play a crucial role in the heat transfer enhancement in rib-roughened cooling channels.
The researchers concluded that advanced post-processing techniques are essential to understand the interaction between coherent structures and the thermal field.
The targeted application of the research is the internal cooling of turbine blades in gas turbine engines.
The experimental part of the study focused on measurements of turbulence characteristics and local heat flux calculations.
The numerical part of the study investigated a generic configuration of a straight duct with square ribs, using both RANS and LES approaches.
The LES simulations used appropriate subgrid-scale models for both momentum and heat transfer.
The researchers carefully analyzed the impact of the inlet boundary conditions on the developed flow and thermal fields.
